The Kindred Peoples Congress: Scholars of the small Finnic and Baltic nations have gathered to read papers no great academy would print: Estonian runic songs, Livonian fisherman's vocabulary, Finnish declensions, Latvian dainas - each proof that the small tongues are nations' tongues. The congress ends with a resolution on 'kindred peoples' that the empires file under 'nostalgia'.
We are kindred - let it be said aloud.
Scholars will be scholars.
The Steam Ferry Across the Gulf

A regular steam ferry between Tallinn and Helsinki: fourteen hours across the gulf, cargo decks smelling of herring and tar, third-class benches full of songbooks and smuggled newspapers. The two shores have been neighbors for a thousand years, now they can visit.
Bind the shores together with steel and steam.
Let the gulf stay wide.
Volunteers Across the Ice

The Estonian envoy in Helsinki reads aloud a single sentence - 'Finland stands with her southern kin' - and the hall rises. Within weeks: Finnish officers for the drill yards, surplus rifles in crates marked 'farm machinery', and a thousand volunteers at the Tallinn quay.
One shore will not watch the other burn.
The Åland Question

The islands between the two kingdoms speak Swedish, fortify nobody's waters, and belong - for now - to the Finns. Sweden's newspapers demand a plebiscite, Finland's answer is a sentence that ends discussion: 'We are not in the habit of giving away our coasts.' The powers suggest the islands be demilitarized and everyone save face.
Press the claim - the islands are Swedish.
Accept the compromise - trade for goodwill.
The Old Shore People

On the islands and the coastal strip live the 'coastal Swedes' - fishermen and farmers whose villages were old when the manors were built, who pay taxes and read their sermons in Swedish. Their elders have come with a petition: schools, a pastorate, and leave to be themselves between the two seas.
The old shore shall keep its tongue.
One land, one language.
Scandinavism

At Uppsala and Lund the students have taken up a new toast: 'For Scandinavia!' - one north, three crowns, kinship in blood and law. Denmark's students sing back from Copenhagen, Norway's from Christiania. The kings eye each other over the toast, the professors give it a decade.
Skål for the North!
Kings toast no one.
The Society of Finnish Literature

A society with a statute, a printing budget and a purpose: to publish in Finnish what no commercial press will risk - grammars, songbooks, novels, the first plays written to be acted in the language of the farmhands. Subscription lists cross the whole grand duchy, and each village's collective subscription is a small flag.
Print the language into a nation.
Let the market decide what is printed.
Stockholm Recognizes Helsinki

The Swedish foreign minister's note is two sentences long and worth a century: Sweden recognizes Finland as a free and sovereign state. In Helsinki the church bells ring, in Stockholm the old mapmakers quietly begin new plates.
The brother in the east is free - so say we.
The Tornio Valley Trade

Along the northern river the border has never mattered much to the farmers: butter south, timber north, church on whichever bank has the best priest this decade. The customs men on both sides have reached that rarest of understandings - a schedule of tariffs low enough to leave the smugglers unemployed.
Low duties, warm neighbors.
A toll is a toll.
Butter, Bacon and the Baltic Trade

Swedish capital, Estonian cream and Latvian bacon: the cooperatives of the eastern shore have found their market in Stockholm's groceries, and Stockholm's banks have found their security in the eastern shore's honest ledgers. The Baltic is becoming what it always should have been - a lake with two busy shores.
Trade is the surest treaty.
We can sell to anyone.
The Kindred Congregations

The Finnish-speaking fishermen of the Estonian coast and their Estonian cousins have begun exchanging preachers, hymnals and choir visits across the gulf - each congregation astonished to find its own old songs sung with different words on the far shore. The churches call it ecumenism, the congregations call it family.
One hymnbook, two shores.
Let each parish mind its own psalms.
The Nordic Games

Skates on the frozen bay, skis on the hills above the town: the northern nations have sent their farm boys and clerks to race each other for a silver cup and the honor of the parish. Half the crowd has crossed an icy gulf to be here, and considers it nothing.
Faster, higher, colder!
Stockholm Hears the Song Festivals

The Swedish papers have printed engravings of the Estonian song grounds: tens of thousands in national dress, singing in their own tongue on ground their grandparents could not own. Stockholm's concert societies have invited the choirs across, the invitation is politely political and politically polite.
Send the choirs their invitation.
Music is best kept at home.
The Stockholm Proposal

The council in Stockholm has sent a proposal across the gulf: the North has been united in one crown - and the United Baltic Provinces, Swedish in letters and kin in law, should stand within it. The old dream of the Good Old Swedish Time has returned, in the shape of the era's greatest power. The Estates of the Provinces must answer - a union of the North and the Baltic, or the last word on the matter of spheres.
Vana hea Rootsi aeg - the union of the North is ours to lead!
We are nobody's province - refuse, and let them come.
The Baltic Refusal

The answer from the Provinces is a refusal - plain, public, and proud. The council in Stockholm is stunned, then furious: a sphere is not a suggestion, the ministers say, and what the crown courts it may also take. The army bureaus begin to draw up plans with familiar coastlines on them.
They have overstepped - to arms!
Let the gulf stay wide - but they will remember this.
